note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Acute local reaction after insect sting (patient unsure if bee or wasp); sting to right arm a few minutes prior to consult.
  - Patient reports difficulty breathing and feeling of tongue “weird”; notes possible swelling of lips.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Sting occurred “just a few minutes ago.”
  - Immediate localized redness/rash and puncture mark at sting site. Patient describes current mild breathing difficulty and anxiety; symptoms not progressing during consult.
- ENT symptoms:
  - Throat swelling/closure sensation: denied (no subjective throat closing reported).
  - Voice change/hoarseness: none reported.
  - Dysphagia/odynophagia: none reported.
  - Drooling: none reported.
  - Nasal/ocular symptoms: none reported.
  - Stridor/noisy breathing: none reported.
  - Dyspnea: subjective mild difficulty breathing/anxiety-related sensation; patient states not acutely breathless at time of consult.
  - Distribution of swelling: patient reports slight right-sided lip swelling sensation; clinician could not visually confirm lip swelling. Tongue “feels a bit weird” per patient.
  - Ear/neck symptoms: none reported.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - No history of anaphylaxis.
  - Never been given an EpiPen / no prior epinephrine injection.
  - History of eczema.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergy: penicillin.
  - No current medications documented.
  - No antihistamines taken prior to consult.
- Social/contextual:
  - Patient living alone; working as computer scientist.
  - Has a cat at home.
  - Patient attended the remote consult alone.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution:
  - Right arm: slightly red with puncture mark and localized blotchy rash at sting site; not markedly swollen to clinician’s view.
  - Lips: patient-reported right-sided sensation of swelling; clinician did not observe visible lip swelling.
  - Tongue: patient reports abnormal sensation; no objective swelling observed on remote inspection.
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - Clinician observed normal speech and breathing during consult; no stridor or increased work of breathing noted.
- Mental status and associated features:
  - Patient anxious; otherwise alert and communicative.
- Vitals and examination findings:
  - Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient:
  - Not present; remote consult between clinician and patient only.

Assessment:
- Primary impression: Localized allergic/inflammatory reaction to insect sting (probable wasp/bee) without current evidence of systemic anaphylaxis.
- Justification:
  - Immediate sting then local redness/rash and puncture mark at site; symptoms began within minutes.
  - Patient reports mild subjective breathing difficulty and lip/tongue sensation, but clinician observed normal breathing, no stridor, and no visible lip/tongue swelling.
  - No prior history of anaphylaxis and no prior epinephrine use.
- Conflict noted:
  - Patient reports difficulty breathing and lip swelling sensation, whereas clinician observed normal breathing and no visible lip swelling during the consult.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Advised over-the-counter oral antihistamine: Piriton (chlorphenamine) — recommended one tablet (4 mg) up to six times daily; alternative option of a once-daily antihistamine also discussed (dose/choice of once-daily agent not specified).
  - Advised to seek urgent care (A&E) immediately if symptoms deteriorate or progress rapidly.
  - Advised to consider medical review/antibiotic therapy if the redness at the sting site spreads, becomes hot, or shows signs suggestive of local infection.
- Specific instructions to patient:
  - Monitor for worsening signs: increasing lip/tongue swelling, difficulty breathing, noisy inspiratory breathing (stridor), progressive rash, or any respiratory compromise.
  - If any deterioration occurs, go straight to A and E.
  - If worried or symptoms change, contact the service / return for review; have a low threshold to contact clinician for reassurance.
  - Provided patient with a link to information about anaphylactic reactions (education).
- Escalation criteria / red flags:
  - New or worsening difficulty breathing, throat tightness/closure sensation, voice change/hoarseness, stridor/noisy inspiratory breathing, progressive facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling, syncope/lightheadedness, rapidly spreading rash.
  - If rapid progression: proceed directly to A&E rather than waiting for a scheduled appointment.
- Follow-up:
  - No immediate ENT/allergy referral indicated given this isolated/local reaction.
  - Consider allergy testing or blood testing if recurrent similar reactions occur in future.
  - No epinephrine auto‑injector prescribed at this time; patient has not previously had or been prescribed an EpiPen.
- Emergency contact instructions exact as stated:
  - “If anything changes, if anything deteriorates. Either make an appointment with us, or go straight to A and E.”
  - “If it’s progressing rapidly, it’s better to go straight to A and E.”
  - “If those kind of things happen, get back to us.”
  - “If you're feeling worried, just have a lower threshold for having a chat with us.”

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vitals (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature) not recorded.
  - Objective confirmation of oral/tongue swelling by direct exam (remote visual inspection performed but limited).
  - No documentation of whether an epinephrine auto-injector is available at home.
  - No explicit current medication list or regular medications documented.
  - No documentation of pulse oximetry or observation period noted.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Patient reports breathing difficulty and perceived lip swelling versus clinician’s observation of normal breathing and no visible lip or tongue swelling (“conflict noted”).
- Transcript quality:
  - Transcript clear and audible; clinical details adequately documented.
